claim: Touch-sensitive stamens are found in hundreds of flowering plants.
source: Touch-sensitive stamens, which are found in hundreds of flowering plants, are thought to function in enhancing pollen export and reducing its loss, but experimental tests are scarce.
evidence: This is stated as background information in the abstract without specific data or citations provided in this sentence.

claim: Stamens of Berberis and Mahonia are inserted between paired nectar glands.
source: Stamens of Berberis and Mahonia are inserted between paired nectar glands and when touched by an insect's tongue rapidly snap forward so that their valvate anthers press pollen on the insect's tongue or face.
evidence: This is a morphological observation supported by Figure 1E showing the anatomical arrangement.

claim: When touched by an insect's tongue, stamens of Berberis and Mahonia rapidly snap forward.
source: Stamens of Berberis and Mahonia are inserted between paired nectar glands and when touched by an insect's tongue rapidly snap forward so that their valvate anthers press pollen on the insect's tongue or face.
evidence: This describes the observed mechanical response of the stamens.

claim: Forward-snapping stamens press pollen on the insect's tongue or face.
source: Stamens of Berberis and Mahonia are inserted between paired nectar glands and when touched by an insect's tongue rapidly snap forward so that their valvate anthers press pollen on the insect's tongue or face.
evidence: This describes the outcome of the stamen movement.

evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental manipulation.

claim: Animals visit flowers to forage for food or other rewards, mainly nectar or pollen.
source: Animals visit flowers to forage for food or other rewards, mainly nectar or pollen (Ollerton, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ollerton, 2021.

claim: Paternity is maximized if pollen grains from one flower are deposited on multiple conspecific recipients, rather than ending up as food.
source: From the perspective of male reproductive success, nectar and pollen are entirely different rewards because paternity is maximized if pollen grains from one flower are deposited on multiple conspecific recipients, rather than ending up as food, while nectar is produced as pollinator food (Westerkamp, 1996; Westerkamp and Classen-Bockhoff, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Westerkamp, 1996 and Westerkamp and Classen-Bockhoff, 2007.

claim: Nectar is produced as pollinator food.
source: From the perspective of male reproductive success, nectar and pollen are entirely different rewards because paternity is maximized if pollen grains from one flower are deposited on multiple conspecific recipients, rather than ending up as food, while nectar is produced as pollinator food (Westerkamp, 1996; Westerkamp and Classen-Bockhoff, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Westerkamp, 1996 and Westerkamp and Classen-Bockhoff, 2007.

claim: A plant's success as a father can depend on its temporal deployment of pollen and on the accuracy of pollen placement on the most effective pollen vectors.
source: A plant's success as a father can depend on its temporal deployment of pollen and on the accuracy of pollen placement on the most effective pollen vectors (Harder and Thomson, 1989; Armbruster et al., 2014, and studies cited therein).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Harder and Thomson, 1989 and Armbruster et al., 2014.

claim: Flowers are under selection to 'pay' visitors as much as possible by nectar, which can usually be replenished.
source: Flowers are therefore under selection to 'pay' visitors as much as possible by nectar, which can usually be replenished, and to meter out their non-replenishable pollen grains by placing them on multiple high-fidelity vectors.
evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary theory and the cited literature.

claim: Flowers are under selection to meter out their non-replenishable pollen grains by placing them on multiple high-fidelity vectors.
source: Flowers are therefore under selection to 'pay' visitors as much as possible by nectar, which can usually be replenished, and to meter out their non-replenishable pollen grains by placing them on multiple high-fidelity vectors.
evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary theory and the cited literature.

claim: Plants achieve pollen metering by filtering their visitors, such that pollen consumers are repelled.
source: Two ways in which plants achieve this are by filtering their visitors, such that pollen consumers are repelled, or by encouraging pollinators to move on, resulting in less pollen and/or nectar consumption per flower while retaining pollen import and export (male and female fitness).
evidence: This describes a general mechanism in plant-pollinator interactions.

claim: Plants achieve pollen metering by encouraging pollinators to move on, resulting in less pollen and/or nectar consumption per flower while retaining pollen import and export.
source: Two ways in which plants achieve this are by filtering their visitors, such that pollen consumers are repelled, or by encouraging pollinators to move on, resulting in less pollen and/or nectar consumption per flower while retaining pollen import and export (male and female fitness).
evidence: This describes a general mechanism in plant-pollinator interactions.

evidence: This is a historical reference citing Linnaeus, 1755.

claim: Berberis flowers have six petals and six stamens, each inserted between two nectaries.

claim: Different species of Berberis and Mahonia vary in the rapidity of their stamen movements.
source: Different species of Berberis and Mahonia, a close relative, vary in the rapidity of their stamen movements and also in the extent of recovery and repeatability, but the first movement of single stamen is generally completed in fractions of seconds (Percival, 1965; Lechowski and Białczyk, 1992; Lebuhn and Anderson, 1994; this study).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and data from the current study.

claim: Different species of Berberis and Mahonia vary in the extent of recovery and repeatability of stamen movements.

evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and data from the current study.

claim: The first movement of a single stamen in Berberis and Mahonia is generally completed in fractions of seconds.

evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and data from the current study.

claim: Early workers thought that the unidirectional stamen movements to the flower center played a role in self-pollination.
source: Early workers thought that the unidirectional stamen movements to the flower center, where the stigma is located, played a role in self-pollination (e.g., Linnaeus, 1755; Sprengel, 1793), but since about the 1880s, it has generally been assumed that the stamen movement helps to precisely pack pollen on the tongues or faces of flies or bees (Kirchner, 1911; Knoll, 1956; Percival, 1965; Kugler, 1970; Lebuhn and Anderson, 1994).
evidence: This is a historical claim supported by citations to Linnaeus, 1755 and Sprengel, 1793.

claim: Since about the 1880s, it has generally been assumed that the stamen movement helps to precisely pack pollen on the tongues or faces of flies or bees.
source: Early workers thought that the unidirectional stamen movements to the flower center, where the stigma is located, played a role in self-pollination (e.g., Linnaeus, 1755; Sprengel, 1793), but since about the 1880s, it has generally been assumed that the stamen movement helps to precisely pack pollen on the tongues or faces of flies or bees (Kirchner, 1911; Knoll, 1956; Percival, 1965; Kugler, 1970; Lebuhn and Anderson, 1994).
evidence: This is a historical claim supported by multiple citations.

claim: Self-pollen receipt by stigmas of B. julianae after a single stamen movement was 14 ± 3 grains (N = 16).
source: Self-pollen receipt by stigmas of B. julianae after a single stamen movement (14 ± 3 grains, N = 16) was only 6% of the pollen receipt resulting from a single visit by the most common visitors, Apis cerana, which deposited between 230 and 260 grains (section 'Effects of forward-snapping stamens on visitor behavior and pollination in the 22 field and under-enclosed conditions') and roughly 1% of the pollen grains of a single anther with its two pollen sacs (ca. 1220 grains), indicating that intra-flower self-pollination mediated by the stamen movements plays a minor role in total pollen receipt.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experiments.

claim: Apis cerana deposited between 230 and 260 grains on stigmas in single visits to B. julianae.
source: Self-pollen receipt by stigmas of B. julianae after a single stamen movement (14 ± 3 grains, N = 16) was only 6% of the pollen receipt resulting from a single visit by the most common visitors, Apis cerana, which deposited between 230 and 260 grains (section 'Effects of forward-snapping stamens on visitor behavior and pollination in the 22 field and under-enclosed conditions') and roughly 1% of the pollen grains of a single anther with its two pollen sacs (ca. 1220 grains), indicating that intra-flower self-pollination mediated by the stamen movements plays a minor role in total pollen receipt.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experiments.

claim: B. julianae was visited mainly by five insect species at the study site.
source: At our study site, B. julianae was visited mainly by five insect species (Supplementary file 2), the bee A. cerana Fab., 1793 (Figure 1A), two anthophorid bees Anthophora waltoni Cockerell, 1910, and Habropoda sichuanensis Wu, 1986 (Figure 1B), and the syrphid flies Rhingia campestris Meigen, 1822, and Meliscaeva spec.
evidence: This is an observational result from field studies.

claim: The bees visiting B. julianae foraged for nectar, but not pollen.
source: These bees foraged for nectar, but not pollen, while the flies fed on both nectar and pollen (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an observational result from field studies shown in Figure 1.

claim: The flies visiting B. julianae fed on both nectar and pollen.
source: These bees foraged for nectar, but not pollen, while the flies fed on both nectar and pollen (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an observational result from field studies shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Pollen transfer efficiency of the bees was significantly higher than that of the flies visiting B. julianae.
source: Consistent with these feeding habits, pollen transfer efficiency of the bees was significantly higher than that of the flies (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study.

claim: Visitation rates of A. cerana to B. julianae did not differ between untreated flowers with mobile stamens (SM), flowers with immobilized stamens (SI) via alcohol immersion, and untreated flowers in a fixed position above alcohol (SMA flowers).
source: Visitation rates of A. cerana to B. julianae (under enclosed conditions) did not differ between untreated flowers with mobile stamens (SM), flowers with immobilized stamens (SI) via alcohol immersion, and untreated flowers in a fixed position above alcohol, called SMA flowers (Wald χ2 = 0.194, df = 2, p=0.908; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a statistical result from experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A. cerana stayed longer in SI compared to SM and SMA flowers of B. julianae.
source: However, A. cerana stayed longer in SI compared to SM and SMA flowers (Wald χ2 = 64.599, df = 2, p<0.001; Figure 3B), showing that it was the forward-snapping stamen that caused these bees to leave.
evidence: This is a statistical result from experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The forward-snapping stamen caused A. cerana bees to leave flowers more quickly.
source: However, A. cerana stayed longer in SI compared to SM and SMA flowers (Wald χ2 = 64.599, df = 2, p<0.001; Figure 3B), showing that it was the forward-snapping stamen that caused these bees to leave.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental comparison.

claim: Visitation rates of A. cerana to B. julianae did not differ among SM, SI, and filament-damaged (FD) flowers.
source: Visitation rates of A. cerana to B. julianae (again under enclosed conditions) also did not differ among SM, SI, and filament-damaged (FD) flowers (Wald χ2 = 0.44, df = 2, p=0.802; Figure 3C) because all three types of flowers offered the nectar sought by these bees.
evidence: This is a statistical result from experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: All three types of flowers (SM, SI, and FD) offered the nectar sought by A. cerana bees.
source: Visitation rates of A. cerana to B. julianae (again under enclosed conditions) also did not differ among SM, SI, and filament-damaged (FD) flowers (Wald χ2 = 0.44, df = 2, p=0.802; Figure 3C) because all three types of flowers offered the nectar sought by these bees.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and bee behavior.

claim: Bees stayed less time in SM flowers than in flowers without stamen bending (SI and FD flowers).
source: However, bees stayed less time in SM flowers than in flowers without stamen bending (SI and FD flowers) and equally long in SI and FD flowers (Figure 3D), showing that it was the stamen forward-snapping per se that caused visitors to move on.
evidence: This is a result from experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Bees stayed equally long in SI and FD flowers.
source: However, bees stayed less time in SM flowers than in flowers without stamen bending (SI and FD flowers) and equally long in SI and FD flowers (Figure 3D), showing that it was the stamen forward-snapping per se that caused visitors to move on.
evidence: This is a result from experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The stamen forward-snapping per se caused visitors to move on from flowers.
source: However, bees stayed less time in SM flowers than in flowers without stamen bending (SI and FD flowers) and equally long in SI and FD flowers (Figure 3D), showing that it was the stamen forward-snapping per se that caused visitors to move on.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental comparison between different flower types.

source: Despite the longer visits, fewer pollen grains were loaded onto A. cerana after a single visit to SI flowers than to SM flowers (716 ± 85 vs. 1223 ± 100 grains in 2020; 890 ± 73 vs. 1401 ± 134 grains in 2021; Wald χ2 = 12.873, p<0.001 in 2020; Wald χ2 = 10.511, p=0.001 in 2021), and the numbers of pollen grains deposited on stigmas by a single A. cerana visit also were much lower in SI flowers than in SM flowers (87 ± 10 vs. 230 ± 25 grains in 2020; 63 ± 8 vs. 260 ± 35 grains in 2021; Wald χ2 = 26.847, p<0.001 in 2020; Wald χ2 = 40.042, p<0.001 in 2021; Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: Fewer pollen grains were loaded onto A. cerana after a single visit to SI flowers (890 ± 73) than to SM flowers (1401 ± 134) in 2021.
source: Despite the longer visits, fewer pollen grains were loaded onto A. cerana after a single visit to SI flowers than to SM flowers (716 ± 85 vs. 1223 ± 100 grains in 2020; 890 ± 73 vs. 1401 ± 134 grains in 2021; Wald χ2 = 12.873, p<0.001 in 2020; Wald χ2 = 10.511, p=0.001 in 2021), and the numbers of pollen grains deposited on stigmas by a single A. cerana visit also were much lower in SI flowers than in SM flowers (87 ± 10 vs. 230 ± 25 grains in 2020; 63 ± 8 vs. 260 ± 35 grains in 2021; Wald χ2 = 26.847, p<0.001 in 2020; Wald χ2 = 40.042, p<0.001 in 2021; Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from field experiments in 2021.

claim: The numbers of pollen grains deposited on stigmas by a single A. cerana visit were much lower in SI flowers (87 ± 10) than in SM flowers (230 ± 25) in 2020.
source: Despite the longer visits, fewer pollen grains were loaded onto A. cerana after a single visit to SI flowers than to SM flowers (716 ± 85 vs. 1223 ± 100 grains in 2020; 890 ± 73 vs. 1401 ± 134 grains in 2021; Wald χ2 = 12.873, p<0.001 in 2020; Wald χ2 = 10.511, p=0.001 in 2021), and the numbers of pollen grains deposited on stigmas by a single A. cerana visit also were much lower in SI flowers than in SM flowers (87 ± 10 vs. 230 ± 25 grains in 2020; 63 ± 8 vs. 260 ± 35 grains in 2021; Wald χ2 = 26.847, p<0.001 in 2020; Wald χ2 = 40.042, p<0.001 in 2021; Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from field experiments in 2020 shown in Figure 5.

claim: The numbers of pollen grains deposited on stigmas by a single A. cerana visit were much lower in SI flowers (63 ± 8) than in SM flowers (260 ± 35) in 2021.

claim: The study found support for the hypothesis that touch-sensitive stamens make pollinators leave more quickly, thus reducing nectar costs per pollen grain movement.
source: This allowed us to test three hypotheses explaining the adaptive value of touch-sensitive stamens in Berberidaceae: visitor filtering; making pollinators leave more quickly, thus reducing nectar costs per pollen grain movement; and precise metering out of few pollen grains per visitor, enhancing pollen export. We found support for the last two, but not for the filtering hypothesis, since flies and bees reacted similarly to stamen bending.

claim: Recent reviews of the adaptive significance of the movement of floral parts have distinguished four types of stamen movement.
source: Recent reviews of the adaptive significance of the movement of floral parts (including both styles and stamens) have distinguished four types of stamen movement: (1) slow movement triggered by a visitor, (2) quick or even explosive movement (sometimes via a catapult mechanism) triggered by a visitor, (3) simultaneous slow movement occurring without triggering by a visitor, and (4) a 'cascade' or staggered movement in which one stamen moves after the other, regardless of triggering (Ren, 2010; Ruan and da Silva, 2011; Armbruster et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ren, 2010; Ruan and da Silva, 2011; and Armbruster et al., 2014.
